title: Forecasting the weather: using today's sky to tell tomorrow's

summary.text: Nobody can see tomorrow, yet weather forecasts are right on most days. A forecast is a careful guess about the weather to come, made from what the air is doing now. Clouds, the wind and damp air are signs of what is coming. Old weather sayings are how people remembered these signs. Some sayings work, some work only in one place, and some do not work at all. Weather moves across the land and sea, so the weather heading your way is already somewhere else today. Weather offices, such as the India Meteorological Department, collect readings from all over the world and use computers to work out how the air will move. Forecasts get less sure the further ahead they look, because small things nobody measured grow bigger.
summary.art: A girl on a city balcony in Chennai looking east at the sea, where tall clouds are building far away. On the railing beside her, a notebook with three columns of ticks, and a phone showing a rain cloud symbol.

intro.hook: Look out of the window now. Will it rain here in the next three hours? Say yes or no. Now say what you looked at to decide.
intro.text: You have just made a weather forecast. A forecast is a guess about the weather to come, made from what you can see and measure now. Fishers, farmers and grandmothers have done this for thousands of years by reading the clouds and the wind. Today, weather offices do it with satellites and computers. In this unit you make a forecast every evening for a week, and check it the next day. You race your forecasts against the weather app, and against the simplest guess of all: 'tomorrow will be like today'. You also find out why some weather sayings work and others do not.
intro.art: A child at a window with their chin on their hands, looking at a sky with a few fluffy clouds, a question mark drawn on the misty glass.

outcomes: I can name signs that help forecast the weather: kinds of clouds, which way the wind blows, and how damp the air is.
I can test a weather saying, and decide from evidence whether it works.
I can make a forecast for tomorrow, check it the next day, and keep a fair score.
I can explain that weather moves across land and sea, so tomorrow's weather is often somewhere else today.
I can explain what 'a 60% chance of rain' means.
I can explain why a forecast for next week is less sure than a forecast for tomorrow, and how weather warnings save lives.

explanations.definition: A weather forecast is a guess about the weather to come, made from measurements of the weather now and knowledge of how weather changes.
explanations.description: A forecast is not magic and it is not a promise. Every forecast starts from the present: what the clouds, the wind, the warmth and the damp air are doing right now, here and in places nearby. Then the forecaster asks how all of this will change. The simplest forecast is 'tomorrow will be like today'. It is right surprisingly often, because weather usually changes slowly. A good forecaster has to beat this simple guess. The hard and useful part is catching the days when the weather is about to change.
examples: In a hot, dry Chennai March, 'tomorrow will be like today' is almost always right.
The day before the monsoon rains reach Kerala, 'tomorrow will be like today' gets it wrong. Watching the clouds and the wind gets it right.
explanations.art: A girl writing two columns in a notebook, 'today' and 'tomorrow', with an arrow from a cloud in the first column to a cloud in the second.
explanations.context: This card says what a weather forecast really is: a careful guess that starts from today's weather.

explanations.definition: Different kinds of cloud form in different kinds of air, so the kind of cloud you see tells you something about the weather to come.
explanations.description: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water or tiny bits of ice, floating in the air. Small puffy cumulus clouds that stay small usually mean fine weather. Cumulus clouds that grow taller and taller during a hot afternoon can become a cumulonimbus, a storm cloud with thunder and heavy rain. A grey sheet of low cloud that covers the whole sky often brings long, steady rain. Thin wisps of cirrus, very high up, are made of ice. When cirrus slowly spreads and thickens into a sheet, a big storm system may be coming, a day or more ahead. No cloud is a sure sign. Each one makes some weather more likely.
examples: Fluffy clouds that stay small all afternoon: probably no rain today.
A cloud tower building fast over the hills behind Coimbatore in the afternoon: a thunderstorm may come within an hour or two.
High streaks of cirrus thickening into a milky sheet: rain may come in a day or two.
explanations.art: Four clouds in a row, each with a small label: small puffy cumulus, a tall cumulonimbus tower, a flat grey rain sheet, and high wispy cirrus.
explanations.context: This card shows how the kind of cloud in the sky helps you forecast the weather.

explanations.concept: Damp air as a weather sign
explanations.definition: Humidity is how much water vapour is in the air. Before rain, the air usually becomes more humid.
explanations.description: Water vapour is water as an invisible gas. Rain is made from water vapour in the air, so humid air is a sign that rain is possible. You can feel humidity. On a humid day, sweat dries slowly, so your skin feels sticky. Washed clothes stay damp for longer. Salt can take in water from damp air, so salt in an open dabba goes lumpy in the rainy season. Hair takes in water too, and curly hair often curls more on humid days. Humid air alone does not mean rain is coming. The damp air must also rise and cool to make clouds and rain.
examples: Salt in an open steel dabba turns lumpy in the monsoon months.
Clothes on the balcony line dry in two hours on a dry day, and stay damp all day when the air is humid.
explanations.art: A steel dabba of salt with lumps in it, beside a balcony where clothes hang limp under grey clouds.
explanations.context: This card explains humidity, the water vapour in the air, and why damp air is a sign that rain is possible.

explanations.definition: Clouds, rain and storms travel across land and sea, carried by winds high in the sky. So the weather coming to you tomorrow is often somewhere else today.
explanations.description: The rain that falls on Chennai today may have been out over the Bay of Bengal yesterday. A storm is a huge swirl of moving air, and the whole swirl travels. The wind you feel on the ground is the air swirling around the storm. That wind can blow one way while the storm itself moves another way. Benjamin Franklin found this in 1743. Clouds high up are often carried by winds that are different from the wind near the ground. This is why weather offices need readings from far away. To forecast tomorrow in Chennai, they need to know what the weather is doing over the sea today.
examples: Before the northeast monsoon rains reach Chennai in October and November, the clouds often build over the Bay of Bengal, to the east.
A thunderstorm seen over the hills to the west of Bengaluru may reach the city an hour later.
explanations.art: A map of South India with a cloud over the Bay of Bengal on 'Day 1', and the same cloud over the coast of Tamil Nadu on 'Day 2', joined by an arrow.
explanations.context: This card explains that weather travels, so what is coming to you is often already somewhere else.

explanations.description: Every part of the world has weather sayings. Some come from careful watching over many years and work well. Some work only in the place where they began. Some mix up a season with a day. And some do not work at all. The only way to know is to test a saying, many times, and count how often it is right. 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight' comes from England, where most weather arrives from the west. A red sunset means the sky to the west is clear, so fine weather is coming. In places where the weather arrives from the east, the same sign can mean something else. Peacocks call loudly and dance in the monsoon. That is their breeding season, which comes with the rains. So the peacock tells you the season, not tomorrow's rain.
examples: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight. Red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning.' An old English saying.
In Tamil Nadu people say 'Aippasi adai mazhai': in the month of Aippasi, which falls in October and November, the rain sets in and does not stop. This matches the northeast monsoon.
Many people say that when ants carry their eggs to higher ground, rain is coming. Few careful tests of this have been done.

perspectives.who: A farmer whose family has watched the sky for generations
perspectives.explanation: Our sayings come from hundreds of years of watching this land. Many of them are right more often than not, and they cost nothing.

Some sayings are right because they describe a real sign, such as high cloud before a storm. But people remember the times a saying worked and forget the times it failed. Only counting, many times over, shows how good a saying really is.

explanations.art: A grandmother and a child on a balcony, with speech bubbles showing a red sunset, a peacock and a line of ants carrying white eggs.
explanations.context: This card is about old weather sayings, and how to tell which ones work.

explanations.definition: Weather offices measure the air all over the world, then use computers to work out how the air will move and change over the next hours and days.
explanations.description: First, they measure. Thousands of weather stations on land, ships and buoys at sea, aircraft, and balloons that rise high into the sky all send readings. Satellites take pictures of the clouds from space, and radars see where rain is falling. Then a weather model, a computer program, uses the rules of how air moves and warms to work out the weather a few minutes ahead, then a few minutes after that, again and again, until it reaches tomorrow and beyond. This needs some of the biggest computers in the world. Finally, meteorologists look at the results, compare them with what they know, and write the forecast. Lewis Fry Richardson, an English scientist, tried to do this by hand during the First World War, and published it in 1922. One forecast, for just 6 hours ahead, took him weeks of work, and it came out very wrong. The first forecast made by an electronic computer was run in 1950.
examples: The India Meteorological Department, set up in 1875, runs weather stations all over India and sends up weather balloons every day.
Indian satellites such as INSAT-3D photograph the clouds over India and the seas around it many times a day.
explanations.art: A loop of pictures: a weather balloon rising, a satellite in space, a big computer, and a woman meteorologist at a screen writing a forecast.
explanations.context: This card explains how weather offices make their forecasts, from measuring to computing to writing.

explanations.definition: A 60% chance of rain means that on 10 days with weather like this, rain would fall on about 6 of them.
explanations.description: The weather never gives a forecaster all the facts. So instead of saying 'it will rain' or 'it will not rain', many forecasts say how likely rain is. A 90% chance means rain is very likely. A 10% chance means rain is unlikely, but it can still happen. If the forecast says 30% and it rains, the forecast was not wrong. Rain on 3 of 10 such days is what 30% means. You only learn whether a forecaster's numbers are good by checking many days. If they say 30% on many days, it should rain on about 3 in 10 of those days.
examples: The app says '70% chance of rain in Mysuru'. Carry an umbrella.
The app said '20% chance of rain', and it rained anyway. That will happen on about 1 in 5 days like this.
explanations.art: A row of 10 small calendar days, 6 with rain clouds and 4 with sun, with '60%' written above them.
explanations.context: This card explains what the percentage in 'chance of rain' means.

explanations.concept: Why forecasts get less sure further ahead
explanations.definition: In weather, tiny differences grow bigger over time. So a small mistake in today's measurements becomes a big mistake in a forecast many days ahead.
explanations.description: No one can measure every bit of air on Earth. Between weather stations there are gaps, and every reading is a little bit off. For tomorrow, these small errors hardly matter. But they grow. After a week, they can turn a sunny forecast into a rainy day. In 1961 Edward Lorenz, an American meteorologist, ran a weather program on his computer twice. The second time he typed in a number rounded off slightly, 0.506 instead of 0.506127. After a while, the two forecasts were completely different. Today a forecast for tomorrow is right most of the time. A forecast for 5 days ahead is good but less sure. For more than about two weeks ahead, nobody can forecast the details of the weather, and most scientists think no one ever will.
examples: Forecasts for 3 to 10 days ahead have improved by about one day each decade. A 6-day forecast today is about as good as a 5-day forecast was ten years earlier.
Weather offices run the same model many times with tiny changes to the starting readings. If all the runs agree, the forecast is surer.
explanations.art: Two lines starting at the same point on a graph and slowly moving apart, ending at a sun on one side and a rain cloud on the other.
explanations.context: This card explains why a forecast for next week is less sure than a forecast for tomorrow.

explanations.definition: A weather warning tells people that dangerous weather, such as a cyclone, very heavy rain or a heat wave, is coming, so they can get ready or move to safety.
explanations.description: Forecasts matter most when the weather is dangerous. In 1999 a very strong cyclone hit Odisha, and about ten thousand people died. In October 2013, the India Meteorological Department tracked Cyclone Phailin for days and forecast where and when it would cross the coast. Close to a million people in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh moved to shelters before the storm hit. The cyclone was about as strong as the one in 1999, but far fewer people died. The India Meteorological Department now gives warnings in colours: green means no warning, yellow means be aware, orange means be prepared, and red means take action. Fishers along the coast are told not to go out to sea when a storm is coming.
examples: A red warning for very heavy rain in Kerala: schools close and people living near rivers move to higher ground.
Ports in India raise warning signals for ships when a storm is near.
explanations.art: A row of people with bags walking into a cyclone shelter on a coast, under a dark swirling sky, with boats pulled up high on the beach.
explanations.context: This card explains how forecasts of dangerous weather save lives.

explanations.description: Many people say animals know when rain is coming. Animals certainly sense changes in the air. Some insects and birds behave differently when the air becomes humid or the wind changes, and many animals take shelter as a storm comes close. Frogs croak loudly after the first monsoon rains, because that is when they find mates. But whether animals can sense rain a day or more ahead is not known. Few careful tests have been done, and people tend to remember the times the animals 'were right'.
examples: Ants pour out of their nest after rain. Do they also move their eggs before it? You could watch and keep count.
Crows and mynas often go quiet and take shelter just before a thunderstorm reaches them.

perspectives.explanation: We have watched animals all our lives. Ants, birds and frogs change what they do before the rains, and they are often right.
Animals sense the weather that is happening now, such as damp air and a rising wind, often more keenly than we do. Whether they can tell what will happen tomorrow has not been shown by careful tests.

explanations.art: A line of ants carrying white eggs up a wall, a crow sheltering under a ledge, and a dark cloud coming.
explanations.context: This card asks whether animals can sense the weather before it comes.

agreed.text: Forecasts for the next day are right most of the time, and forecasts have got better every decade.
agreed.evidence: Weather offices check every forecast against what really happened, and publish how often they were right.

agreed.text: Weather travels. Storms, clouds and rain move across land and sea.
agreed.evidence: Satellite pictures taken every half hour show clouds moving. Weather stations along a coast record a storm arriving at one town after another.

agreed.text: Small differences in the air grow over time, so detailed forecasts many weeks ahead are not possible.
agreed.evidence: Running the same weather model with tiny changes to the starting numbers gives very different weather after about two weeks.

agreed.text: Some cloud signs really do help forecast the weather, such as tall cumulonimbus clouds before a thunderstorm.
agreed.evidence: Weather observers have recorded clouds and the weather that followed for more than two hundred years.

agreed.text: Warnings of cyclones and heavy rain save many lives.
agreed.evidence: Far fewer people died in Odisha in Cyclone Phailin in 2013 than in the cyclone of 1999, which was about as strong, because people moved to shelters in time.

challenging.claim: A weather forecast is only a guess, so it is no use.
challenging.who: Some people, after a forecast went wrong
challenging.for: Forecasts are sometimes wrong, and people remember those days.
challenging.against: A forecast for tomorrow is right on most days, much more often than chance. Even a forecast that is sometimes wrong helps you decide, and warnings of cyclones have saved many thousands of lives.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that forecasts are useless because they are guesses.

challenging.claim: When the forecast said '30% chance of rain' and it rained, the forecast was wrong.
challenging.for: The forecast seemed to say rain was unlikely, and then it rained.
challenging.against: 30% means rain on about 3 of every 10 days like this one. Rain on one such day is what the forecast allowed. To judge the forecast, you need to check many days.
challenging.context: This card is about what a percentage chance of rain really means.

challenging.claim: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight' works everywhere.
challenging.who: An old English saying, now repeated around the world
challenging.for: In England, where most weather comes from the west, a red sunset often means a clear sky to the west and fine weather coming.
challenging.against: The saying depends on which way the weather usually travels. Where weather often arrives from the east, as in Chennai in the northeast monsoon, the sign may not work. Test it where you live.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a weather saying from one country works in another.

challenging.claim: Animals can sense rain a day or more before it comes.
challenging.for: Animals sense humid air and changes in the wind keenly, and many people have seen them act differently before rain.
challenging.against: Careful tests that count the times the animals were wrong, as well as right, are rare. Animals may be reacting to weather that is already changing.
challenging.context: This card is about whether animals can forecast the weather.

challenging.claim: With big enough computers, we will one day forecast the weather a month ahead, day by day.
challenging.who: A hope some people have held
challenging.for: Forecasts have improved by about a day each decade, and computers keep getting faster.
challenging.against: Lorenz showed that tiny differences grow. Most meteorologists think day-by-day detail cannot be forecast beyond about two weeks, however big the computer. Forecasts of a whole season, such as 'a wetter monsoon than usual', are possible, but only as chances.
challenging.context: This card is about how far ahead the weather could ever be forecast.

big_questions.q: Tomorrow's weather grows out of today's air. So is tomorrow already decided, or still open?
big_questions.hint: Think of Lorenz's two runs, which started almost the same and ended completely different.

big_questions.q: A storm's wind blows one way, but the whole storm travels another way. What, then, is a storm: the wind, or the swirl?
big_questions.hint: Stir water in a bucket and then push the bucket. Which way does the water go round, and which way does the bucket move?

big_questions.q: If a forecast says 60% chance of rain, is the forecast right or wrong when it does not rain?
big_questions.hint: Think of 10 days with the same forecast. On how many would you expect rain?

big_questions.q: Grandparents' sayings and the weather office's computer both try to tell tomorrow. How are they alike, and how are they different?
big_questions.hint: Both start from signs. Which one checks itself against what really happened, day after day?

big_questions.q: Why do we remember the times a saying came true more than the times it failed?
big_questions.hint: Think of a time you were sure a saying worked. Did you count the times it did not?

big_questions.q: A butterfly flapping their wings changes the air a tiny bit. Could that change, weeks later, change where a storm goes?
big_questions.hint: Lorenz asked this question in a talk in 1972. Nobody can check it for one butterfly. What does his rounded number show?

story.title: Three Guessers on the Balcony
story.note: Kavya, Arjun, Paati and their flat are made up. The facts are real: Chennai gets most of its rain in the northeast monsoon, from October to December. Rain systems often form over the Bay of Bengal and move west to the coast, and high thin cloud can spread out ahead of them. Salt goes lumpy in damp air.
text: Kavya was nine, and she lived on the sixth floor of a building in Besant Nagar, in Chennai. From the balcony, if she leaned a little, she could see a strip of grey-blue sea between two other buildings. Her little cousin Arjun was staying with them for the October holidays. He was seven, and he had one big wish. On Saturday it would be his birthday, and he wanted to fly his new kite on the beach.
On Thursday evening, Amma looked at the weather app on her phone. 'Saturday: seventy per cent chance of rain,' she read.
'That app is silly,' said Arjun. 'Look at the sky. It's all blue. Saturday will be sunny, like today.'

Paati was sitting on the balcony with her evening tea. She did not look at the phone. She looked east, over the strip of sea. High up, very high, there were thin white streaks, like hairs combed across the sky.
'Mazhai varudhu,' said Paati quietly. Rain is coming.
'How do you know?' asked Kavya. 'There isn't a single dark cloud.'

'Those thin clouds, high up, come before the big rain from the sea,' said Paati. 'My father was a fisherman in Pulicat. He watched them every evening. Sometimes they come and nothing happens. But when they get thicker, day after day, the boats stay on the beach.'

Kavya fetched her notebook. She drew three columns and wrote a name at the top of each: PAATI, THE APP, ARJUN. 'Every evening, all three of you make a forecast for tomorrow,' she said. 'Rain or no rain. The next evening, I check who was right and give a point.'
'I'll win,' said Arjun. 'Tomorrow will be like today. Easy.'

On Friday morning, Kavya ran out to the balcony before brushing her teeth. Thursday's forecasts had been for Friday: Paati said no rain yet, the app said no rain, and Arjun said sunny, like Thursday. Friday was dry and hot. Everyone got a point.

But the sky had changed. The thin streaks had spread into a pale milky sheet, and the sun looked weak through it. That night Kavya saw a big ring of light around the Moon. Paati nodded at it. 'Ice, very high up,' she said. 'The rain is getting closer.'

Something else had changed too. The wind had been blowing from the sea in the afternoons, as usual, but now it kept blowing in the evening, steady and cool, from the northeast. The air felt heavy and sticky on Kavya's arms. When Amma opened the salt dabba to make rasam, she frowned. 'Lumpy,' she said, tapping the spoon. 'The air is wet.'

On Friday evening, Kavya took the forecasts for Saturday. Paati said rain. The app now said ninety per cent chance of rain. Arjun crossed his arms. 'Today was dry,' he said. 'So tomorrow will be dry.'

It started to rain at five o'clock on Saturday morning. It was not a quick shower. It rained all day, steady and grey, and the road below turned into a brown stream. Arjun stood at the balcony door in his birthday shirt, holding his kite and looking at the water.
Kavya gave Paati a point and the app a point. Arjun got nothing. He looked as if he might cry.
'How did the app know?' he asked. 'It hasn't got a Paati.'

Amma showed them the weather office's website on her phone. There was a picture taken from a satellite. A huge white swirl of cloud sat over the Bay of Bengal, right next to the coast of Tamil Nadu. Amma pressed a button, and the picture played the last three days like a film. On Wednesday the swirl had been far out at sea. On Thursday it was closer. On Friday it was spreading towards the coast. Today it was over them.

Kavya stared at it. 'So Saturday's rain was already there on Thursday,' she said slowly. 'It was just out at sea. Paati saw the edge of it, the high thin clouds. The app saw the whole thing from space.'
'And I only looked at our sky,' said Arjun. 'Our sky was blue.'

'Your way isn't silly,' said Kavya, because she could see he was upset. 'Look at my notebook. On Friday you were right too. Weather doesn't change most days. When it doesn't, you win. You only lose on the days it changes.'
'And those are the days that matter,' said Paati, 'if you are a fisherman. Or a boy with a kite.'

The rain stopped on Monday. On Tuesday the sky was clear, and Arjun flew his kite on the beach. That evening he made his own forecast for Wednesday, but this time he looked east first, over the sea, before he said a word.

Kavya kept the contest going for two whole weeks. At the end, the app had the most points, Paati was close behind, and Arjun was third, but not by much. At the bottom of the page, Kavya wrote one line: 'Tomorrow's weather is today's weather somewhere else, on its way.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: the rain that fell on Saturday was already over the Bay of Bengal on Thursday, and it travelled to the coast. Paati read its first signs: high cirrus cloud spreading ahead of it, a halo around the Moon, a steady wind from the sea, and damp air that made the salt lumpy. The weather app used satellite pictures and computer models to see the whole system. Arjun's 'tomorrow will be like today' is a real forecast, called a persistence forecast. It wins on most ordinary days and loses on the days when the weather changes.
ask: What signs did Paati see before the rain came? Which one would you look for first?
Why was Arjun right on Friday but wrong on Saturday?
How could the app know about the rain before anyone in Chennai could see a rain cloud?
At the end, Arjun looked east before making his forecast. Why east?
Kavya kept score for two weeks, not just one day. Why was that fairer?

rules: Each player gets a set of 4 forecast cards. Shuffle the sign cards and put them face down, with the brackets hidden.
Turn over the top sign card and read it aloud, without the answer in brackets.
Every player chooses one forecast card and puts it face down. Then everyone turns their card over together.
Read the answer in brackets. Everyone who matched it scores 2 points.
If you chose a different card, you can still score 1 point by giving a good reason why your forecast could also happen.
Some cards say 'possible' or 'sometimes'. For those, everyone who says why the sign is not a sure thing scores 1 extra point.
After all 16 cards, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Give each player 4 forecast cards. 3. Shuffle the sign cards and put them face down.
flow.say: In this game, each card shows a sign in the sky or the air. You forecast the weather it points to.
flow.kid: Get your 4 forecast cards. Mix up the sign cards. Put them face down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sky Signs, a card game where you forecast the weather from signs. Here you set it up.

flow.do: Play the first sign card, 'Puffy clouds growing taller and taller on a hot afternoon', as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Puffy clouds are growing taller and taller on a hot afternoon. What's your forecast?
flow.kid: Practice card. Puffy clouds are growing taller on a hot afternoon. What's your forecast?

check.q: Puffy clouds are growing taller and taller on a hot afternoon. What is the best forecast?
check.why: On a hot afternoon, warm damp air rises and builds the clouds taller. If they keep growing, they can become a cumulonimbus storm cloud, with thunder and heavy rain. Choosing 'fine weather' means looking at the puffy shape but not at the growing.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards, keeping score.
flow.say: Next card. Choose your forecast. Ready? Turn it over. Who matched?
flow.kid: Turn the next card. Choose your forecast. Turn them over together. Who matched?
flow.parent: The peacock card is a trick worth talking about. Peacocks call and dance in the monsoon because it is their breeding season. So they tell you the season, not tomorrow's weather.

games.context: This is a board game. A cyclone moves across the Bay of Bengal towards the coast. You are the forecasters, and you must warn four coastal towns before it arrives.

Town cards along the coast: Chennai, Nellore, Puducherry, Cuddalore
Squares 4 and 8: STORM GROWS STRONGER. Move the storm 1 extra square.

printables.title: 20 question cards (answers in brackets)
items: What do we call a huge swirling storm that forms over a warm sea? (A cyclone)
Name one way weather offices see a cyclone far out at sea. (Satellites, or radar, or ships and buoys)
What does an orange weather warning mean? (Be prepared)
What does a red weather warning mean? (Take action)
Why should fishers stay on the beach when a cyclone is coming? (The sea becomes very rough and dangerous)
What does a 90% chance of rain mean? (Rain is very likely: on about 9 of 10 days like this)
Does a storm always travel the way its wind blows? (No)
Who found that a storm can move against its own wind, in 1743? (Benjamin Franklin)
Name a thin, wispy, high cloud made of ice. (Cirrus)
What is humidity? (How much water vapour is in the air)
What is the simplest forecast of all? (Tomorrow will be like today)
Is a forecast for tomorrow surer than one for next week? (Yes)
Why do forecasts get less sure further ahead? (Small errors in today's readings grow bigger)
In which months does Chennai get most of its rain? (October to December, the northeast monsoon)
What does a weather model do? (Works out how the air will move and change, using a computer)
Name the Indian weather office. (The India Meteorological Department)
Which cyclone in 2013 was forecast so well that close to a million people moved to safety? (Cyclone Phailin)
What is a halo? (A ring of light around the Sun or Moon, made by ice crystals high up)
What should a family near the coast do with a red cyclone warning? (Follow the official advice, and move to a shelter if told to)
What cloud brings thunder and lightning? (Cumulonimbus)

On your turn, answer a question card. Right answer: put a 'warned' flag on any town that does not have one yet. Wrong answer: no flag this time.
Playing alone? Read the card yourself and check the answer in the brackets.
After every player has had a turn, roll the dice. On 1, 2 or 3, the cyclone moves 1 square. On 4, 5 or 6, it moves 2 squares.
On a STORM GROWS STRONGER square, the cyclone moves 1 extra square.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board, the town cards and the question cards. 2. Put the cyclone on square 1.

flow.kid: A cyclone is out at sea. You are a forecaster. Warn all four towns before it reaches the coast!
flow.context: This is the first step of Storm Warning, a board game where you warn coastal towns before a cyclone arrives. Here you set it up.

flow.do: Take turns answering cards, placing flags and moving the cyclone.
flow.say: Your question. Right? Put a flag on a town. Now the storm moves. Will we warn everyone in time?
flow.kid: Answer your card. Right? Put a flag on a town. Then roll for the storm.

check.q: Why does warning towns early save lives?
options: People have time to move to safety
check.why: A warning cannot change the storm. It gives people time to move away from the coast, bring boats in and get to shelters. That is how forecasting Cyclone Phailin in 2013 saved so many lives.

flow.do: Talk about the game.
flow.say: In the game, the earlier we saw the storm, the more time we had. How do real forecasters see a cyclone early?
flow.kid: How do real forecasters see a cyclone early?

experiments.title: Tomorrow Like Today? A week-long forecast contest
experiments.question: Whose forecast for tomorrow is right most often: 'tomorrow will be like today', your own reading of the sky, or the weather app?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which of the three forecasters will get the most points in a week? Which will get the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three forecasts are written at the same time each evening, before anyone knows what tomorrow brings. Nobody changes a forecast after writing it. All three are judged on the same two questions, by the same rules. We run the contest for 7 days, because one day can be a fluke.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil, or the printed score sheet
a window or balcony where you can see some sky
a phone with a weather app, or the India Meteorological Department website (mausam.imd.gov.in)
the cloud cards from activity a1, if you made them

experiments.safety: Look at the sky, never straight at the Sun. If there is lightning, watch from indoors, away from the open balcony.

schedule.what: Set up the score sheet. Write down today's weather. Make the first three forecasts for tomorrow.
Check yesterday's three forecasts and give points. Then make three new forecasts for tomorrow.
Check and score. Make tomorrow's forecasts.
Check and score. Make tomorrow's forecasts. Who is ahead so far?
Check and score. Make tomorrow's forecasts.
Check and score. Make tomorrow's forecasts.
Check and score. Make the last forecasts.
Check and score the last day. Add up the points, draw a bar chart and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table every evening. On day 8, add up each forecaster's points and draw a bar for each.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table in the notebook, or print the score sheet. 2. Write the three forecasters at the top: 'Same as today', 'Me', 'The app'. 3. Read out the two questions everyone will answer each evening.
flow.say: We're going to have a forecast contest for a week. Every evening, three forecasters guess tomorrow. The first just says tomorrow will be like today. The second is you, reading the sky. The third is the weather app. Each evening they answer two questions. Will it rain tomorrow? Will the sky be mostly sunny or mostly cloudy?
flow.kid: You are running a forecast contest! Three forecasters guess tomorrow's weather. One says 'same as today'. One is you. One is the weather app. Each answers two questions. Will it rain? Sunny or cloudy?
flow.parent: Agree on the rules now, and write them at the top of the page. Rain means enough rain to wet the balcony floor or the road, at any time from morning to bedtime. 'Mostly cloudy' means clouds cover more than half the sky for most of the day. For the app, a chance of rain of 50% or more counts as 'yes, rain'.
flow.context: This is the first step of the forecast contest. You set up a score sheet for three forecasters, who will each guess tomorrow's weather every evening for a week.

flow.do: Ask your child to predict the winner and give a reason. Write the guess and the reason at the top of the page.
flow.say: Before we start, which forecaster do you think will win the week? Which will come last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the winner. Who will come last? Why do you think so? Write your guess at the top.

ask.q: Why do you think that forecaster will win?
good: The app has satellites and computers.
Weather doesn't change much, so 'same as today' will be right a lot.
I can see the clouds myself.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Don't say which one usually wins. Let the week answer it.

flow.do: 1. Go to the window or balcony. 2. Write today's weather in the 'What really happened' column: rain or no rain, mostly sunny or mostly cloudy. 3. Write the 'Same as today' forecast for tomorrow: just copy today.
flow.say: First, what is today's weather? Did it rain today? Was the sky mostly sunny or mostly cloudy? The first forecaster just copies today for tomorrow.
flow.kid: Look outside. Did it rain today? Was it sunny or cloudy? Write it down. Copy today into the 'Same as today' column for tomorrow.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to look at the sky for two minutes. They notice the clouds, which way they move, and how the air feels. 2. They write their own forecast for tomorrow. 3. Then open the weather app and write its forecast for tomorrow.
flow.say: Now it's your turn. Look carefully. Are there clouds? What kind? Are they growing or shrinking? Is there wind? Does the air feel sticky? Now make your forecast for tomorrow. Then we'll write what the app says.
flow.kid: Look at the sky for two minutes. What clouds? Is there wind? Is the air sticky? Write your forecast for tomorrow. Then write the app's forecast.

ask.q: What did you see that made you choose your forecast?
good: The sky is clear and there is no wind.
The air is sticky, so rain might come.

flow.parent: Always write your child's forecast before looking at the app, so the app does not change their mind. That keeps the test fair.
flow.wait: Every evening for the next 6 evenings, at about the same time, do steps s5 and then s3 and s4 again.

flow.do: 1. Each evening, look at yesterday's three forecasts. 2. Give each forecaster 1 point for a right rain answer, and 1 point for a right sunny or cloudy answer. 3. Then make the three new forecasts.
flow.say: Let's check yesterday's forecasts against what really happened today. One point for the right rain answer, and one point for the right sky answer. Who scored today?
flow.kid: Check yesterday's forecasts. Was each one right about rain? About sun or cloud? Give 1 point for each right answer.

check.q: Yesterday, 'Same as today' said 'no rain, sunny'. Today it rained, and the sky was cloudy all day. How many points does 'Same as today' get?
check.why: Both answers were wrong. It said no rain, but it rained. It said sunny, but it was cloudy. So 0 points. This is the kind of day when the weather changes, and 'same as today' always misses a change.

flow.parent: On day 4, look at the totals together. Who is ahead? Is it what your child guessed?

flow.do: On day 8, after the last check: 1. Add up each forecaster's points. The most anyone can get is 14. 2. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each forecaster.
flow.say: The contest is over. Let's add up the points. The most anyone could get is 14, because there were 7 days and 2 points a day. Now let's draw a bar for each forecaster.
flow.kid: The contest is over! Add up each forecaster's points. The most is 14. Draw a bar for each one.
flow.parent: If every day was the same weather, all three may have scored 14. That is a real result, not a failed test. In a settled spell, 'same as today' is very hard to beat. If you can, run the contest again when the weather is changing, for example at the start of the monsoon or in October and November.

flow.do: Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning. Then explain, if your child has not said it already, why 'same as today' does well and when it fails.
flow.say: What did you find? Who won? Which days did each forecaster get wrong? What was happening on those days?
flow.kid: Who won? Which days did each forecaster get wrong? What was the weather doing on those days?

ask.q: On the days 'Same as today' was wrong, what had happened?
good: It rained after a dry day.

ask.q: How do you think the app knew about a change before it happened?
good: It sees the clouds coming from far away.
The weather was already somewhere else.

flow.parent: The usual pattern: weather changes slowly on most days, so 'same as today' scores well. It fails exactly when the weather changes. A good forecast earns its keep by catching those changes, and it can only do that by seeing the weather that is on its way, somewhere else. If your child's own forecasts beat 'same as today', ask which signs helped.

experiments.context: In this week-long experiment, you run a forecast contest. Every evening three forecasters guess tomorrow's weather: 'tomorrow will be like today', you, and the weather app. Then you find out who is right most often.

experiments.title: Salt in the Steamy Bathroom: does damp air change salt?
experiments.question: Many people say salt goes lumpy before rain. Does damp air really change salt?
experiments.predict: Guess first. One plate of salt goes into a steamy bathroom, and one goes into a dry room. After one hour, will they look and feel different? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind of salt, the same amount and the same kind of plate. Only the place changes: the steamy bathroom or a dry room. Leave both for the same time, then test both in the same way.
results_table: Does it slide off when tilted? (yes, some, no)
How it feels when pressed with a finger

materials.item: plain table salt (powdered salt, not big crystals)
two flat steel plates of the same size
a teaspoon
a bathroom just after a hot bath or shower, with the door and window shut
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up runs the hot water. Hot water and hot taps can scald. Don't eat the salt afterwards: throw it away or use it to scrub a vessel.

schedule.what: Put one plate of salt in a steamy bathroom and one in a dry room. Wait one hour. Tilt both plates and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both plates. Draw both plates after tilting, showing where the salt stayed.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 level teaspoon of salt on each steel plate. 2. Spread it into a thin, even patch about the size of a biscuit. 3. Tilt each plate a little to check the dry salt slides.
flow.say: Here are two plates with the same salt, spread the same way. Watch what dry salt does when I tilt the plate.
flow.kid: Put one spoon of salt on each plate. Spread it thin. Tilt a plate. See how dry salt slides?
flow.context: This is the first step of the salt test. You put the same salt on two plates, to find out whether damp air changes it.

flow.do: Ask your child to predict, with a reason.
flow.say: One plate goes into the bathroom after a hot bath, where the air is full of steam. The other goes into a dry room. What will the salt be like after an hour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One plate goes in the steamy bathroom. One goes in a dry room. What will happen in an hour? Why?

ask.q: Why might the bathroom change the salt?

flow.do: 1. Just after a hot bath or shower, put plate 1 on a dry bathroom shelf, away from splashes. 2. Shut the door and window and turn off any exhaust fan. 3. Put plate 2 in the driest room, away from the kitchen.
flow.say: The bathroom air is full of water vapour from the hot water. We shut the door to keep it in. The other plate goes where the air is dry.
flow.kid: Put plate 1 on a dry shelf in the steamy bathroom. Shut the door. Put plate 2 in a dry room.
flow.parent: Put the plate where no water can splash or drip on it, so only the damp air reaches the salt. On a very humid monsoon day, the dry room may not be very dry. Then put plate 2 in a room with an air conditioner, or just compare with fresh salt from the dabba.

flow.do: 1. Bring both plates out together. 2. Look closely at each. 3. Tilt each plate slowly until it is nearly upright. 4. Press the salt gently with a finger.
flow.say: Let's compare. Look first. Now tilt each plate slowly. Does the salt slide off? Now press it gently with a finger. How does it feel?
flow.kid: Bring both plates. Look closely. Tilt each one slowly. Does the salt slide? Press it gently. How does it feel?

ask.q: What is different about the bathroom salt?
good: It is stuck to the plate.

flow.parent: Usually the bathroom salt looks darker and wetter, sticks to the plate and clumps together, while the dry-room salt slides off. If you see no difference, put the bathroom plate back and leave it overnight with the door shut, or try on a very humid monsoon day.

flow.do: Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning. Then explain humidity and what this means for the saying.
flow.say: What did you find? What took in the water? So, does lumpy salt tell us that rain is coming?
flow.kid: What did you find? Where did the water come from? Does lumpy salt mean rain is coming?

check.q: The bathroom salt went lumpy. Where did the water come from?
options: Water vapour in the damp air
check.why: The plate was kept away from splashes, so the water came from the damp air. Salt takes in water vapour from humid air. Lumpy salt tells you the air is humid. Humid air makes rain possible, but it does not promise rain. The air must also rise and cool to make rain clouds.

flow.parent: The saying has a true part: salt really does show that the air is damp, and damp air often comes before rain. But damp air does not always bring rain. A strong answer says both.

experiments.context: In this experiment you test an old saying, that salt goes lumpy before rain. You compare salt left in a steamy bathroom with salt left in a dry room.

experiments.title: Ground Wind and Cloud Wind: do they go the same way?
experiments.question: Does the wind on your balcony blow the same way as the clouds high above are moving?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the clouds move the same way as the wind on your balcony? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same spot each time. Check the ground wind with the same ribbon and the clouds against the same fixed edge. Check on 3 different days, because one day can be a fluke.
results_table: Ground wind comes from (north, south, east or west)

materials.item: a strip of thin plastic bag or a light ribbon, about 30 cm long
a pencil, stick or ruler to tie it to
a phone with a compass app, or know which way the Sun rises (east)
a fixed edge to watch clouds against: a window frame, a wall top, a water tank or a building
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: Hold the stick inside the balcony railing. Never lean over a railing or climb onto anything. Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Make the wind ribbon. Check the ground wind and the cloud direction. Write both down.
Check both again, at about the same time.
Check both again. Compare all three days.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw an arrow for the ground wind and an arrow for the clouds on a little compass drawing.

flow.do: 1. Tie the plastic strip or ribbon to the end of the pencil. 2. Find north on the phone compass, or face where the Sun rises, which is east. 3. Write N, E, S and W on a page as a cross.
flow.say: We'll make a wind ribbon to see which way the air is moving on our balcony. First, let's find north, east, south and west.
flow.kid: Tie the ribbon to the pencil. Find north with the phone. Draw a cross. Write N, E, S, W.
flow.context: This is the first step of the wind test. You make a wind ribbon, then compare the wind on your balcony with the way the clouds are moving.

flow.do: Ask for a prediction with a reason.
flow.say: Do you think the clouds high up will move the same way as the wind here? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the clouds move the same way as the wind here? Why?

flow.do: 1. Hold the ribbon out at arm's length, inside the railing. 2. The ribbon streams away from where the wind comes from. 3. Write where the wind comes from.
flow.say: Hold it still. The ribbon points away from where the wind comes from. So if it streams towards the west, the wind is coming from the east.
flow.kid: Hold the ribbon out, inside the railing. Which way does it stream? The wind comes from the other side. Write it down.
flow.parent: Stay with your child on the balcony. Buildings bend the wind, so if the ribbon flaps about in all directions, try a different side of the balcony or an open window on another side.

flow.do: 1. Pick a cloud close to a fixed edge, such as the top of a building. 2. Keep your head still and watch for one minute. 3. Which way does it move? Write where the clouds come from.
flow.say: Clouds move slowly, so we watch one against something that stays still. Keep your head still. Is the cloud moving away from the edge or towards it?
flow.kid: Pick a cloud near the top of a building. Keep your head still. Watch for one minute. Which way does it move?
flow.parent: Thin high clouds can be hard to read. Lower, puffy clouds are easiest. If there are no clouds at all, try again another day.

flow.do: On day 3, compare the three days. Ask for a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: On how many days did the clouds go the same way as the ground wind? What does that tell you about the air high up?
flow.kid: Look at all three days. Same or different? What does it tell you about the wind high up?

check.q: On your balcony the ribbon shows wind from the east, but the clouds are coming from the west. What does that tell you?
options: The air high up is moving a different way from the air near the ground
check.why: Clouds are carried by the wind high up, which can blow a different way from the wind near the ground. This is why Franklin's storm could move against its own ground wind. To forecast, you watch which way the clouds come from, not only which way the ground wind blows.

flow.parent: In the afternoon in coastal cities like Chennai, a sea breeze often blows in from the sea near the ground, while clouds above move a different way. Any result is fine. The idea is that the air has layers that move differently.

experiments.context: In this experiment you check whether the wind on your balcony blows the same way as the clouds are moving high above. Forecasters watch both.

activities.title: Read the Sky Now: your first forecast

materials.item: a window or balcony with some sky
paper and coloured pencils
a clock

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Look at the sky, make a forecast for the next three hours, and check it later.

activities.record: Draw the sky now. Write your forecast and the time. Three hours later, write what really happened.

flow.do: 1. Go to the window or balcony together. 2. Ask your child to say everything they notice about the sky and the air, without naming any weather yet.
flow.say: What do you notice about the sky right now? What colour is it? Are there clouds? What do they look like? Can you feel any wind? How does the air feel on your skin?
flow.kid: Look at the sky. What colour is it? Are there clouds? What shape? Is there wind? How does the air feel?

good: A big dark cloud over there.

flow.context: This is the first step of a quick activity. You look closely at the sky now, so that you can make your first weather forecast.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw the sky. 2. Ask them for a forecast for the next three hours: rain or no rain, and what the clouds will do. 3. Write down the time.
flow.say: Draw the sky as it is now. Now make a forecast. In three hours, will it be raining? Will there be more cloud or less? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Draw the sky now. What will it be like in three hours? Rain or no rain? More clouds or fewer? Why?

ask.q: What made you choose your forecast?
good: It's clear, so it will stay dry.

flow.do: Three hours later, look again. Write what happened next to the forecast.
flow.say: It's been three hours. Let's look. Was your forecast right? What changed? What did you see earlier that could have told you?
flow.kid: Three hours later, look again. Were you right? What changed?
flow.wait: Wait three hours, then do this step.
flow.parent: Don't worry about whether the forecast was right. The habit we want is to look closely, guess with a reason, and check.

flow.say: Older people often know signs and sayings about the weather. Let's ask Paati. You ask the question, and I'll help you write.

flow.kid: Sort the sayings. Which ones are a sign you can watch for? Which ones are about a season?

good: Watch for the sign and see if rain comes the next day.
Count how many times it is right.
Write it down every time we see the sign.

activities.title: Six Out of Ten: what 'chance of rain' means

materials.item: 6 rajma beans (red) and 4 white chana or 4 white buttons, all about the same size
a steel tumbler or a cloth bag you cannot see into
paper and pencil

activities.safety: Children under 4 must not play with beans, because they can choke. Don't eat the raw beans.

schedule.what: Pick beans from a tumbler without looking, 10 times, to see what '60% chance of rain' means.

activities.record: Draw 10 boxes for 10 days. In each box draw a rain cloud for a rajma and a sun for a chana.

flow.do: 1. Put 6 rajma and 4 chana in the tumbler. 2. Explain: each rajma is a day it rains, each chana is a dry day.
flow.say: Here are 10 beans. 6 red rajma stand for rain, and 4 white chana stand for no rain. This tumbler is like a forecast that says 60% chance of rain.
flow.kid: Put 6 rajma and 4 chana in the tumbler. Rajma means rain. Chana means dry. This is a 60% chance of rain.
flow.context: This is the first step of an activity with beans. You use rajma and chana in a tumbler to understand what '60% chance of rain' means.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes the tumbler, picks one bean without looking, and draws a cloud or a sun in box 1. 2. They put the bean back and shake again. 3. Repeat for all 10 boxes.
flow.say: Each pick is one day with the same forecast. Pick without looking. Rain or dry? Now put it back, so the chance stays the same, and pick again.
flow.kid: Shake. Pick one bean without looking. Rajma? Draw a cloud. Chana? Draw a sun. Put it back. Do it 10 times.

ask.q: Before you pick, can you tell whether this 'day' will be rainy?
good: No, but rain is more likely.
Rajma is more likely, because there are more of them.

flow.do: Count the rain days. Talk about what happened.
flow.say: How many of your 10 days had rain? Was it exactly 6? If the forecast said 60%, and one day stayed dry, was the forecast wrong?
flow.kid: Count your rain days. Was it exactly 6? If one day was dry, was the forecast wrong?

check.q: The forecast said '60% chance of rain', and it did not rain. What does that tell you?
options: Dry days happen on about 4 of 10 days like this, so it is not a surprise
A 60% forecast means it will rain for 60 minutes
check.why: A 60% chance means rain on about 6 of 10 days like this, and no rain on about 4. A dry day is one of those 4. To judge a forecaster, you would check many days. Thinking it means 60 minutes of rain is a common mix-up.

flow.parent: Your child may get 5, 6, 7 or even 8 rain days out of 10. That is normal with chance. Doing it again gives a different count. Over many tries, it comes close to 6 in 10.

projects.title: Our Family Book of Weather Sayings, Tested

materials.item: the sayings collected in activity a2
a notebook, or 4 sheets of paper folded and stapled into a booklet
coloured pencils

projects.safety: Watch the sky from indoors or a balcony. Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Choose two sayings that give a sign you can watch for. Make a tally page for each.
Watch for both signs each evening. If you see one, mark it. The next day, mark whether the weather it promised came.
Count the tallies. For each saying, decide: keep it, keep it with a warning, or drop it. Write and draw the book.

projects.record: On each tally page: the saying, the sign, the weather it promises, and two rows of tally marks: 'sign seen, and the weather came' and 'sign seen, but the weather did not come'.

flow.do: 1. Choose two sayings that give a sign you could see in the next two weeks. 2. On a page for each, write the saying, the sign, and what it promises. 3. Draw two rows for tally marks: 'came true' and 'did not come true'.
flow.say: Let's choose two sayings to test. We need a sign we might really see, like high streaks of cloud or lumpy salt. For each one, we'll count the times it came true and the times it did not.
flow.kid: Pick two sayings. Write each on its own page. Draw two rows: came true, did not come true.
flow.parent: Good sayings to test in a flat: 'Thin streaks high in the sky mean rain in a day or two', 'Lumpy salt means rain is coming', 'Tall clouds in the afternoon mean thunder by evening'. A saying about a season, such as the rains in Aippasi, cannot be tested in two weeks. Keep it in the book as a season saying.
flow.wait: Each evening for two weeks, look for the signs. The next day, mark a tally.
flow.context: This is the first step of a two-week project. You test two family weather sayings by counting how often they come true, and make a book of what you find.

flow.do: Each evening, look for both signs. The next day, add a tally mark.
flow.say: Did we see the sign yesterday? Did the weather it promised come today? Let's add a mark.
flow.kid: Did you see the sign yesterday? Did the weather come today? Add a tally mark.
flow.parent: Only add a mark on days the sign was seen. If a sign never appears in two weeks, that is a result too: write it down and keep testing later.

flow.do: 1. Count the tally marks for each saying. 2. Decide: keep it, keep it with a warning, or drop it. 3. Write and draw each saying on a page of the book, with the count and the decision.
flow.say: Let's count. How many times did each saying come true? How many times not? Should we keep it in our book, keep it with a warning, or drop it? Why?
flow.kid: Count the marks. Did the saying come true more often than not? Keep it, keep it with a warning, or drop it?

ask.q: One saying came true 2 times and failed 1 time. Is that enough to trust it?
good: We need to test it more.

flow.parent: With only a few tallies, the honest answer is often 'not sure yet'. That is how real science sounds. Keep the book and add to it in the next season.

challenges.title: Warn the Boats
challenges.problem: Fishing boats from a village on the coast are out at sea, far beyond phone signal. The weather office has just warned that a storm is coming. Design a way to warn the boats to come back.
constraints: The warning must be seen or heard from far out at sea.
It must work by day and by night.
It must be easy to understand for everyone, whatever language they speak.
materials: a steel plate and a spoon
general: Boat radios: fishers listen to weather warnings on the radio.
Flags or shapes raised high on a pole by day, and lights by night. Ports in India use warning signals like this for ships.
A loud siren or bell on the shore.
creative: A code of torch flashes: long and short flashes that mean 'come back now'.
A chain: the nearest boat that hears the warning passes it on to the next boat, and so on.
A bright coloured kite or balloon flown high above the shore.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own warning. Draw it, make a model or act it out. Test it: stand at one end of the longest room or corridor and see if your family can understand it from the other end.

flow.parent: If testing in a corridor or stairwell of a building, stay with your child. Torches are good for testing at night with the lights off.

flow.kid: See what real ports use. What would you change in your design?

ask.q: Why must a warning come early?
good: The boats need time to get back.
The storm is moving towards them.

Use the forecast, but remember it gives chances, not promises.

Take an umbrella or a raincoat just in case.
Check the forecast again on Sunday morning, because a forecast for the next few hours is surer.
