quiz.p: Meera, a girl in Class 3 in Coimbatore, sees puffy clouds growing taller and taller on a hot afternoon. What weather is most likely soon?
quiz.why: Growing cumulus clouds can become cumulonimbus storm clouds, which bring thunder and heavy rain. Picking a dry answer means seeing the clouds but not noticing that they are growing.

opts: A careful guess about the weather to come, made from what the air is doing now
quiz.why: A forecast starts from today's weather and works out how it will change. It is a careful guess, not a promise.

quiz.p: Shalini, a girl in Mysuru, says, 'My grandmother's saying worked last Tuesday, so it always works.' What is the best way to check?
opts: Ask more people whether they like the saying
Watch for the sign many times and count how often the weather it promises really comes
Look it up in a storybook
quiz.why: One time can be luck. Counting the times a saying comes true and the times it fails, over many tries, shows how good it is.

quiz.p: In a forecast contest, 'tomorrow will be like today' got most days right. On which kind of day did it go wrong?
opts: On days when the weather stayed the same
On days when the weather changed
quiz.why: 'Same as today' always predicts no change. So it is right when the weather stays the same and wrong every time it changes. Catching those changes is what makes a forecast useful.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Chennai, sees a big swirl of cloud on a satellite picture over the Bay of Bengal, moving towards the coast. What is the best forecast for Chennai?
opts: Rain may come soon, because the cloud is moving towards the city
No rain, because the sky over Chennai is blue now
The cloud will stay where it is
quiz.why: Weather travels. A storm moving towards the coast today may reach the city tomorrow, even if the sky over the city is still blue.

quiz.p: Benjamin Franklin's storm had a wind from the northeast. Which way did the storm itself travel?
opts: Towards the northeast, against its own wind
Towards the southwest, with its wind
quiz.why: Franklin found the storm reached Boston, to the northeast, hours after Philadelphia. A storm's winds swirl around it, while the whole storm travels another way.

quiz.p: The forecast says '70% chance of rain'. What does it mean?
opts: 70% of the city will get wet
On 10 days like this, rain would fall on about 7
quiz.why: A 70% chance means rain on about 7 of 10 days like this one. It does not mean minutes or how much of the city gets wet.

quiz.p: The forecast said '20% chance of rain', and it rained. Was the forecast wrong?
opts: Not necessarily: rain happens on about 2 of 10 days like this
quiz.why: 20% means rain is unlikely but possible. Rain on 2 of every 10 such days is what 20% means. You would need to check many days to judge the forecaster.

quiz.p: Why is a forecast for next week less sure than a forecast for tomorrow?
opts: Weather offices try less hard for next week
Small errors in today's measurements grow bigger over time
Computers switch off after one day
Next week's weather is decided by the Moon
quiz.why: Nobody can measure every bit of air. The small errors grow day by day, as Edward Lorenz found with his rounded number. So forecasts get less sure the further ahead they look.

quiz.p: What does a red weather warning from the India Meteorological Department mean?
quiz.why: Green means no warning, yellow means be aware, orange means be prepared, and red means take action, for example moving to safety.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Kochi, leaves salt on a plate in a steamy bathroom for an hour. The salt goes lumpy. What does this show?
opts: Salt takes in water vapour from damp air
quiz.why: Salt takes in water vapour from humid air and goes lumpy. Lumpy salt shows the air is damp, which makes rain possible, though not certain.

quiz.p: Why do weather offices need readings from far away to forecast your city's weather?
opts: Because the weather coming to your city is often somewhere else today
Because far-away readings are more exciting
Because your city has no weather
Because computers only work with far-away numbers
quiz.why: Weather travels across land and sea. To know what is coming, forecasters need to know what the air is doing in the places it is coming from.

items.p: Match each cloud to what it often tells you.
pairs: Small puffy clouds that stay small
A tall cloud with a flat, spreading top
A low grey sheet over the whole sky
Thin high streaks that thicken day by day
rain in a day or two
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the four cloud signs in this unit. A strong answer also says that no cloud is a sure sign, only a likely one.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Chennai, wants to know if it will rain tomorrow. What is the best thing to look at?
opts: What day of the week it is
The clouds, the wind and how damp the air feels
items.why: Clouds, wind and damp air are signs of what is coming. What day of the week it is tells you nothing about the weather.

items.p: Water in the form of an invisible gas is called water ____.
items.why: Water vapour is water as a gas. Humidity is how much water vapour is in the air.

items.p: Divya says, 'A forecast is a promise about tomorrow.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A forecast is a careful guess made from today's weather. It is right most days, but not every day. A strong answer says what a forecast really is.

items.p: In the forecast contest, why does 'tomorrow will be like today' get so many days right?
items.a: Because on most days the weather changes slowly, so tomorrow is often like today.
items.why: A strong answer says weather usually changes slowly, and adds that this forecast always gets it wrong when the weather does change.

items.p: Sort these into 'a sign of weather coming soon' or 'a sign of the season'.
items: clouds growing tall on a hot afternoon
Weather coming soon
peacocks calling loudly in July
The season
a ring around the Moon
Weather coming soon
frogs croaking after the first monsoon rains
The season
salt gone lumpy in the dabba
Weather coming soon
thin high streaks thickening into a sheet
Weather coming soon
items.a: see items
items.why: Clouds, a halo and lumpy salt are about the air now and the next day or two. Peacocks calling and frogs croaking happen every monsoon, because that is their breeding season. A strong answer explains why each animal sign belongs to the season.

items.p: Draw the sky you would expect an hour before a thunderstorm. Label the kind of cloud.
items.art: An empty sky over a row of city buildings.
items.a: A tall cumulonimbus cloud with a dark bottom and a flat, spreading top, labelled.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a cloud that is much taller than it is wide, and labels it a cumulonimbus or storm cloud.

items.p: Ramesh, a boy in Hyderabad, puts salt on a plate in a steamy bathroom. After an hour, what will the salt most likely be like?
opts: Lumpy and sticking to the plate
items.why: Salt takes in water vapour from the damp air. So it goes lumpy and sticks to the plate.

items.p: Two sisters in Madurai are planning tomorrow.

views.says: Today was sunny, so tomorrow will be sunny. That's what usually happens.
Look at those thin streaks getting thicker. I think rain is coming.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Use what you found in the forecast contest. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence, for example from the forecast contest. It sees that Asha is right on most ordinary days, and that Bhavana's way can catch the days when the weather changes. A very strong answer suggests using both.
items.why: Both sisters are partly right. 'Same as today' wins on settled days and loses when the weather changes.

items.p: Three of these come from measuring or watching the weather. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A satellite, a weather balloon and a weather station all measure the air. A horoscope does not measure anything about the weather.

items.p: Put the steps of making a forecast at a weather office in order.
items: The computer works out how the air will move
Meteorologists check the results and write the forecast
Measure the air all over the world
Send the readings to a big computer
a: Measure the air all over the world
Send the readings to a big computer
The computer works out how the air will move
Meteorologists check the results and write the forecast
items.why: First measure, then send, then compute, then check and write. A strong answer says why each step needs the one before.

items.p: Nila says, 'The wind on our balcony always blows the same way the clouds are moving.' Is she right?
items.why: False. The wind high up, which carries the clouds, can blow a different way from the wind near the ground. A strong answer mentions the wind ribbon test.

items.p: Sita, a girl in Kozhikode, hears that the weather office has given an orange warning for heavy rain. What does orange mean?
items.why: Yellow means be aware, orange means be prepared, red means take action.

items.p: Write one weather saying you know or collected. Say how you could test whether it works.
items.a: Any saying, with a test that watches for the sign many times and counts how often the promised weather comes.
items.why: A strong answer counts both the times the saying came true and the times it did not, over many days.

items.p: Label the four parts of the forecast contest score sheet: the three forecasters and what really happened.
items.art: A blank table with four empty column headings and seven rows.
items.why: A strong answer also says why 'What really happened' is filled in the next day, never before.

items.p: A ring of light around the Moon, made by ice crystals in thin high cloud, is called a ____.
items.why: A halo forms when moonlight or sunlight passes through tiny ice crystals high in the sky. It often appears in the thin cloud that spreads ahead of a big storm system.

items.p: Franklin's storm blew from the northeast, but travelled towards the northeast. Explain how both can be true.
items.a: The wind swirls around the storm, while the whole storm moves along. So the wind at one place can blow one way while the storm travels another way.
items.why: A strong answer separates the wind inside the storm from the movement of the whole storm, perhaps using the picture of water swirling in a bucket that is pushed along.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Visakhapatnam, sees on the satellite film that a cloud swirl is 300 km out at sea and moving towards the coast at about 100 km each day. When might it arrive?
items.why: 300 km at 100 km a day takes 3 days. A strong answer adds that storms can speed up, slow down or turn, so the forecast must be checked again each day.

items.p: Kiran says, 'If the forecast said 30% chance of rain and it rained, the forecast was wrong.' Is he right?
items.why: False. 30% means rain on about 3 of 10 days like this. Rain on one of those days is what the forecast allowed. To judge a forecaster, you check many days.

items.p: In the salt test, the plate in the bathroom was kept away from splashes. Why did that matter?
items.a: So that the only water reaching the salt was water vapour from the air, not drops from the tap.
items.why: A strong answer says this made the test fair: it showed the damp air, not splashes, changed the salt.

items.p: A thunderstorm builds on a hot afternoon in Bengaluru. Put what happens in order.
items: Puffy clouds grow taller and taller
A tall storm cloud brings thunder and rain
The sun heats the ground in the morning
Warm, damp air rises
a: The sun heats the ground in the morning
Puffy clouds grow taller and taller
A tall storm cloud brings thunder and rain
items.why: Heat, then rising damp air, then growing clouds, then the storm. A strong answer says why the storm comes in the afternoon, not the early morning.

items.p: Edward Lorenz ran his weather program twice. The second time he typed 0.506 instead of 0.506127. What happened?
opts: Both forecasts came out the same
After a while, the two forecasts were completely different
The second forecast was always better
items.why: The tiny difference grew until the two forecasts were completely different. This is why detailed forecasts many weeks ahead are not possible.

items.p: Sort these sayings and signs: 'worth testing', 'about a season, not tomorrow', or 'cannot be about weather'.
items: salt goes lumpy before rain
Worth testing
in Aippasi the rain does not stop
About a season
it rains when you forget your umbrella
Cannot be about weather
a ring around the Moon means rain soon
Worth testing
peacocks dance when the rains come
About a season
ants carry their eggs up before rain
Worth testing
items.a: see items
items.why: A sign in the air or sky is worth testing. A sign that happens every monsoon tells you the season. Something with no link to the air cannot tell you the weather. A strong answer gives a reason for each.

items.p: Three people in a fishing village near Rameswaram are deciding whether to go to sea tomorrow.

views.who: Mariamma, a fisherwoman who sells the catch
views.says: The weather office has given an orange warning. We should keep the boats on the beach.
The sky looks clear and the wind is gentle. My eyes have never failed me.
If we stay ashore every time there is a warning, we lose a day's money. The forecast was wrong last month.

items.ask: Whose view would you follow? Give your reasons. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer chooses whom to trust most and gives reasons, for example that the weather office sees storms far out at sea. Then it answers back from another view: the grandfather's signs are free and quick, and the young fisher is right that the app can be wrong. A very strong answer says to use the warning and the signs together, and to stay ashore if either says danger.
items.why: There is a real trade-off between staying safe and losing a day's catch. Warnings and local signs work best together.

items.p: A weather office needs readings from the sea, from the sky and from other countries to forecast for your city. Explain why.
items.a: Weather travels, so the weather coming to my city tomorrow is somewhere else today, perhaps over the sea or another state.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that weather moves, with an example such as rain coming from the Bay of Bengal to Chennai.

items.p: The simplest forecast, 'tomorrow will be like today', is called a ____ forecast.
items.why: Persistence means staying the same. Meteorologists use it to check whether their own forecasts are any better.

items.p: In the wind ribbon test, the ribbon streams towards the west. Where is the wind coming from?
items.why: The ribbon streams away from where the wind comes from. So it points west when the wind blows from the east.

items.p: Draw a map with a storm over the sea and your city on the coast. Draw where the storm is today, and where you forecast it will be tomorrow.
items.art: A blank outline of a coast with the sea on one side.
items.a: A storm drawn over the sea, an arrow, and the storm drawn again nearer to or over the city.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the storm moving, with an arrow, and labels 'today' and 'tomorrow'.

items.p: Rukmini says, 'Lumpy salt means it will certainly rain tomorrow.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Lumpy salt shows the air is humid. Humid air makes rain possible, but rain also needs the damp air to rise and cool into rain clouds.

items.p: Match each tool to what it tells forecasters.
pairs: the air high above the ground
where rain is falling right now
how the air will move next
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool measures a different part of the weather. A strong answer says why forecasters need all of them.

items.p: In Kavya's forecast contest, the app won. Arjun says, 'So I should never use my own eyes.' Do you agree? Why or why not?
items.a: No. The app is usually best, but your own eyes see what is happening right now where you are, such as a storm cloud growing, which can help the app's forecast.
items.why: A strong answer sees that both have a use: the app sees far away, and your eyes see right here and right now.

items.p: Kavya's score sheet for 'Same as today' shows: day 1, 2 points. Day 2, 2 points. Day 3, 0 points. Day 4, 1 point. Day 5, 2 points. How many points in all?
items.why: 2 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 7. A strong answer also says what probably happened on day 3, the day the weather changed.

items.p: Zainab, a girl in Pune, says, 'If we measured every bit of air on Earth perfectly, we could forecast the weather a year ahead.' What do you think? Use Lorenz's story.
items.a: Perhaps for a while, but even the tiniest bit of air we missed, or rounded off, would grow. We can never measure every bit perfectly, so forecasts a year ahead will never be possible day by day.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rounded number 0.506 and says that tiny differences grow, and that perfect measurement is not possible in practice.

items.p: Two meteorologists disagree about the monsoon.

views.who: Dr Revathi, who forecasts the weather
views.says: We cannot say whether it will rain in Chennai on 15 July. Nobody can forecast the weather so far ahead.

views.who: Dr Prakash, who forecasts the monsoon season
views.says: But we can say in April whether the whole monsoon is likely to bring more rain or less than usual.

items.ask: Can they both be right? Explain how. Then say which forecast a farmer planning what to plant would want, and why.
items.a: A strong answer explains that a forecast for the whole season can be given as a chance, such as 'more rain than usual is likely', while a day-by-day forecast for July cannot be made in March. Both have a point.
items.why: This is a real difference between forecasting the weather on one day and forecasting a whole season. Both are done, in different ways.

items.p: A weather office runs its model 50 times, each time with tiny changes to the starting readings. 45 of the runs show heavy rain on Friday. What should the forecast say?
opts: Heavy rain is very likely on Friday, about a 90% chance
items.why: 45 out of 50 is 90 out of 100, so heavy rain is very likely. Running the model many times shows how sure a forecast is.

items.p: Why might a saying that works well in England fail in Chennai? Use 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight' as your example.
items.a: In England most weather comes from the west, so a red sunset means clear sky to the west and fine weather coming. In Chennai, rain often comes from the east, from the Bay of Bengal, so the sunset sky in the west tells you less.
items.why: A strong answer links the saying to the direction weather usually travels from in each place.

items.p: The forecast contest in a hot, dry March ended in a tie: all three forecasters got 14 points. Is this a useless result? Explain.
items.a: No. It shows that when the weather does not change, 'same as today' is as good as anything. To find out which forecaster is best, we would need to test when the weather is changing.
items.why: A strong answer treats the tie as real evidence, and suggests a better time for a second test.

items.p: In 1999 a very strong cyclone hit Odisha and about ten thousand people died. In 2013 Cyclone Phailin was about as strong, but far fewer died. Give two reasons forecasting helped.
items.a: The storm was tracked for days, so people knew where and when it would hit. Close to a million people moved to shelters in time, and boats were brought in.
items.why: A strong answer names knowing early and acting on the warning. A very strong answer says the forecast was only useful because people trusted it and acted.

items.p: Lewis Fry Richardson, an English scientist, worked out a 6-hour forecast by hand about a hundred years ago. It took him weeks. Why was it not useful, even if it had been right?
opts: The weather had already happened long before he finished
items.why: A forecast must arrive before the weather does. A 6-hour forecast that takes weeks to work out arrives long after the weather has happened. Fast computers solved this.

items.p: Your ribbon showed wind from the east, but the clouds came from the west. Which tells you more about where tomorrow's rain might come from?
opts: The way the clouds are moving
items.why: Clouds are carried by the wind high up, so the way the clouds move shows where the weather is coming from. The ground wind is bent by buildings and the sea breeze.

items.p: Many people say, 'Ants carry their eggs to high ground before rain.' Design a fair test of this saying in your building. What would you watch, how often, and for how long?
items.a: Find an ant trail near the building. Every evening for a month, note whether ants are carrying eggs upward. Next day, note whether it rained. Count all four kinds of day: eggs and rain, eggs and no rain, no eggs and rain, no eggs and no rain.
items.why: A strong answer counts the days the ants were wrong as well as the days they were right, and tests for many days.

items.p: Gauri says, 'A forecast for 5 days ahead today is about as good as a 4-day forecast was ten years ago.' Is she right?
items.why: True, roughly. Forecasts for 3 to 10 days ahead have improved by about one day each decade, thanks to better measurements, faster computers and better models.

items.p: Draw two lines on a graph that start at almost the same point and slowly spread apart. Label one end 'sunny' and the other 'storm'. Write one sentence saying what the drawing shows.
items.art: A blank graph with 'Days ahead' along the bottom.
items.a: Two lines starting together and spreading apart, with a sentence such as 'Tiny differences at the start grow into big differences later.'
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lines very close at first and far apart at the end, and the sentence names Lorenz's finding.

items.p: Sort these forecasts: 'very likely to be right' or 'much less sure'.
items: Rain in the next hour, with a storm cloud overhead
Very likely to be right
Sunny tomorrow in a dry March
Very likely to be right
Rain on a day three weeks from now
Much less sure
The exact temperature a month from today
Much less sure
A cyclone crossing the coast tomorrow, tracked for 4 days
Very likely to be right
Thunder on a birthday two months away
Much less sure
items.a: see items
items.why: Forecasts for the next hours and tomorrow are much surer than forecasts weeks ahead. Seasonal forecasts give only chances. A strong answer says why time matters.

items.p: Nobody can see tomorrow. So how is it possible to forecast the weather at all? Answer in your own words.
items.a: Because tomorrow's weather grows out of today's. The air that will bring it is already moving somewhere today, so by measuring today we can work out tomorrow.
items.why: A strong answer links today and tomorrow, and mentions that the weather is moving towards us from somewhere else. A very strong answer also says why this gets harder further ahead.

items.p: Put these forecasts in order of how sure they are, from most sure to least sure.
items: Rain in 5 days
Rain on a day next month
Rain in the next 10 minutes, when it is starting to drizzle
Rain tomorrow, with a storm moving in from the sea
a: Rain in the next 10 minutes, when it is starting to drizzle
Rain tomorrow, with a storm moving in from the sea
Rain on a day next month
items.why: The closer in time, the surer the forecast, because small errors have had less time to grow.

items.p: Label the parts of a weather office's forecasting chain on this picture: the satellite, the weather balloon, the computer and the meteorologist.
items.art: A drawing of a satellite in space, a balloon rising from the ground, a big computer and a woman at a desk, joined by arrows, with four empty label lines.
items.why: A strong answer says what each part does: the satellite and balloon measure, the computer works out how the air will move, the meteorologist checks and writes the forecast.

open_questions.q: How far ahead could the weather ever be forecast, even with perfect computers?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists say about two weeks for day-by-day detail, but the exact limit is still argued about, and it may be different for different kinds of weather.

open_questions.q: Can animals really sense rain coming a day or more ahead?
open_questions.why_open: Many people have seen animals behave differently before rain, but careful tests that count the misses as well as the hits are rare.

open_questions.q: Why are some monsoon seasons much wetter or drier than others?
open_questions.why_open: The sea temperatures of the Pacific and Indian Oceans play a part, but scientists cannot yet fully explain or forecast every monsoon.

open_questions.q: Exactly where will a thunderstorm form this afternoon?
open_questions.why_open: Forecasts can say storms are likely in an area, but the exact street where one will build up is still very hard to forecast.

open_questions.q: Could a tiny change, like a butterfly's wings, really change where a storm goes weeks later?
open_questions.why_open: Lorenz's work shows tiny differences can grow, but no one can test it for one real butterfly. Scientists still argue about how far this idea goes in the real atmosphere.

maths.problem: In the forecast contest, the app scored 12 points out of 14, and 'Same as today' scored 10. How many more points did the app score?
maths.explain: The app scored 12 and 'Same as today' scored 10. 12 take away 10 is 2. So the app scored 2 more points. That means the app caught one more change in the weather, worth 2 points, or two changes worth 1 point each.
maths.context: This is about the forecast contest, where three forecasters guess tomorrow's weather every evening for a week and score points.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the scores tells you how much better one forecaster did, not just which one won.

maths.problem: Draw a bar chart of these contest scores: Same as today 10, Me 11, The app 12. Which bar is tallest? How much taller is it than the shortest?
maths.answer: The app's bar is tallest. It is 2 points taller than 'Same as today'.
maths.explain: Draw three bars, 10, 11 and 12 high. The app's is tallest at 12. The shortest is 'Same as today' at 10. 12 minus 10 is 2.
maths.context: This is about the forecast contest. After 7 days, you add up each forecaster's points.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance who did best, and how close the race was.

maths.problem: Priya, a girl in Thiruvananthapuram, put 6 rajma and 4 chana in a tumbler, then picked one bean without looking. Is she more likely to pick rajma or chana? What if she put in 2 rajma and 8 chana?
maths.answer: With 6 rajma and 4 chana, rajma is more likely. With 2 rajma and 8 chana, chana is more likely.
maths.explain: With 6 rajma out of 10, rajma is more likely than chana. It is like a 60% chance of rain. With 2 rajma out of 10, chana is much more likely. That is like a 20% chance of rain: rain is unlikely, but it can still happen.
maths.context: This is about the bean tumbler activity, where rajma stand for rainy days and chana for dry days.
maths.why_maths: Chance of rain is a forecast in numbers. Knowing what makes something likely or unlikely helps you read a forecast.

maths.problem: In one week of Kavya's contest it rained on 3 of the 7 days. What fraction of the days had rain? Did more than half the days have rain?
maths.answer: 3 sevenths of the days had rain. That is less than half.
maths.explain: 3 rainy days out of 7 days is 3 out of 7, written 3/7. Half of 7 is three and a half, and 3 is less than that. So fewer than half the days had rain.
maths.context: This is about the forecast contest, where you write down every day whether it rained.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you how often something happened, which is the first step to saying how likely it is.

maths.problem: A thunderstorm is 30 km away and moving towards your town at 10 km each hour. How long until it arrives, if it keeps going the same way?
maths.explain: Each hour it moves 10 km closer. After 1 hour it is 20 km away, after 2 hours 10 km, after 3 hours 0 km. So it arrives in 3 hours. 30 divided by 10 is 3.
maths.context: This is about weather moving. Forecasters track storms on radar and work out when they will arrive.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how far away a storm is and how fast it moves tells you how much time you have to get ready.

roots.context: We have learned to make forecasts from clouds, wind and damp air, and to check them. Now we ask what forecasting tells us about time, and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: Every forecast in your contest was made from that evening's sky and readings. The weather that came next was already in the air somewhere, moving towards you. So the better we measure today, over a wider area, the further ahead we can see.
deep_truth.habit: We think of tomorrow as hidden and cut off from today, something only a fortune-teller could see. But tomorrow's weather grows out of air that exists today, so knowing tomorrow comes from reading today carefully and widely.
deep_truth.evidence: In the forecast contest, every guess, even the weather app's, used only what could be seen or measured that evening. Franklin's storm and the Bay of Bengal rains show weather reaching one place after being somewhere else. Lorenz's rounded number shows the limit: what nobody measured grows.

three.who_am_i: You are a forecaster. Every time you look at the sky and take an umbrella, you are reading today to guess tomorrow.
three.what_is_life: Farmers, fishers, ants and birds all live by the weather. Knowing what is coming helps every living being get ready.
three.what_is_this_world: The air around the whole Earth is one moving ocean. The air on your balcony now was somewhere else this morning.

roots.thread: There is one layer of air wrapped around the whole Earth, always moving. It shows up as many weathers: a hot still afternoon in Madurai, a storm over the Bay of Bengal, snow in Ladakh. They are all the same air, warmed and cooled in different places. Because it is one moving whole, the weather in one place tomorrow grows out of the weather in other places today. That is why a forecast for one city needs readings from all over the world.

teachings.source: Tirukkural, chapter 2, 'The Excellence of Rain', verse 11
teachings.teaching: The world goes on living because of rain. So rain should be thought of as amrita, the nectar of life.
teachings.link: Rain mattered so much to farmers that people watched the sky every day and made sayings to remember its signs. Forecasting began from that care.

teachings.source: The Buddha's teaching of dependent arising, in the Samyutta Nikaya 12.21
teachings.teaching: When this is, that comes to be. From the arising of this, that arises.
teachings.link: Tomorrow's rain arises from today's warm sea, rising damp air and wind. A forecast follows these causes forward, one step at a time.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, the Greek philosopher, as reported by Plato in the Cratylus (402a)
teachings.teaching: Everything moves on and nothing stays still. You cannot step into the same river twice.
teachings.link: The air never stays still. The air you breathe on the balcony this evening will be far away tomorrow, and new air will have taken its place.

science.text: Weather models start from measurements of the air now and work forward using the rules of how air moves and warms.
Tiny differences in the air grow over time, so detailed weather cannot be forecast more than about two weeks ahead.
Exactly how far ahead the weather could ever be forecast, even with perfect computers, is still argued about.

other_view.view: Tomorrow is not simply sitting in today's air waiting to be read. Tiny changes that no instrument could ever measure grow into big ones, so the weather a month from now is truly open. Today's air shapes the next few days, but it does not fix the far future.

practice.title: Where was this air this morning?
practice.say: Let's stand at the window or on the balcony. Close your eyes. Feel the air on your face and arms. Is it moving? Which side of your face feels it most? Now take three slow breaths. This air was somewhere else this morning. Maybe it was over the sea, or over another street. Tomorrow it will be somewhere else again. Open your eyes. Which way do you think it is going?
practice.kid: Stand at the window. Close your eyes. Feel the air on your face. Which side feels it most? Breathe slowly three times. This air was somewhere else this morning. Where is it going now?

ask: If you could measure every bit of air on Earth tonight, could you know tomorrow's weather for sure?
The air on your balcony now was somewhere else this morning. Where does 'our' weather begin and end?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. The forecast contest needs only a notebook, some sky and the weather app, and a parent's phone is enough. It gives a different result in different seasons: in a dry, settled spell all three forecasters can tie, and the step says this is a real result and suggests running it again when the weather is changing. The rules for 'rain' and 'mostly cloudy' are fixed at the start, because without them families argue over scores. The child's forecast is always written before the app is opened, so the app cannot sway it. The salt test uses a steamy bathroom after a hot bath, with the door shut and the plate away from splashes. If no change shows after an hour, the step says to leave it overnight or try on a humid monsoon day. The wind ribbon is held inside the railing, with a grown-up present, and the step says to try another window if buildings make the ribbon flap about. Beans are kept from children under 4. The satellite activity needs internet and a grown-up. Both games work for one child alone. how_we_found_out.story: On a November night in 1743, Benjamin Franklin, a printer and scientist in Philadelphia in America, hoped to watch an eclipse of the Moon. A storm came instead. Thick clouds hid the sky, and a strong wind blew from the northeast. In those days, people thought a storm travels the way its wind blows. So Franklin guessed that this storm had come from the northeast, from the direction of Boston, where his brother lived. He thought Boston must have missed the eclipse too. Later, letters and newspapers from Boston surprised him. People there had seen the eclipse clearly, and the storm reached Boston hours after it hit Philadelphia. The storm had moved towards the northeast, against its own wind. Franklin collected reports of later storms from towns along the coast and found the same pattern. A storm's winds swirl around it, while the whole storm travels somewhere else. This also showed something useful. If storms travel, news of a storm can be sent ahead of it. After the telegraph was invented, towns could be warned before a storm arrived.

how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a storm travels in the direction its wind blows. Franklin found that a storm with a northeast wind moved towards the northeast, against its wind, because a storm is a swirl of air that travels as a whole.
